key_takeaways: Shortlist three to five venues, give each one a row in the same spreadsheet, and agree which columns decide it before you look at prices.
Compare capacity per space and per package: one Bali listing gives 150 seated overall, yet its exclusive buyout offer is for up to 60 guests.
Check whether each quote is venue hire or a minimum spend, and whether tax, service charges and local fees are inside it.

Under Australian Consumer Law, an Australian business must not take your payment if it knows, or should know, it cannot supply on time; a change of mind, or a third party stopping the venue, generally runs on the contract, and you should not assume the same rules cover a venue overseas.
Abroad, add columns for a legal ceremony on site, curfews, the wet-weather plan, transfers and local permits, and get every answer in writing.

faq.q: What should a wedding venue comparison spreadsheet include?
faq.a: One row per venue, with identical columns for capacity, dates, exclusive use, price type, inclusions, catering, accommodation, the wet-weather plan, curfews, transfers and deposit terms. Abroad, add whether a legal ceremony can happen on site, and note every answer's source.

faq.q: How many venues should we compare at once?
faq.a: We suggest three to five. Fewer gives you little to measure against; more, and the tours and follow-up emails start to blur. If a venue fails one of your deciding columns, take it off the sheet.

faq.q: What is the difference between a minimum spend and venue hire?
faq.a: Venue hire pays for the space; a minimum spend is a floor on your spend there. Our Dubai cost guide, for example, says some luxury spaces set a minimum spend, from AED 60,000 at a desert resort to AED 120,000 for an outdoor amphitheatre (November 2026), and suggests asking whether a quoted rate includes the 7% municipality fee, 10% service charge and 5% VAT.

faq.q: Can we get our venue deposit back if we cancel?
faq.a: If you cancel by choice, your contract decides. If an Australian venue has a major problem with its service, the ACCC says terms and conditions cannot take away your right to a remedy, but if a third party's actions stopped the venue from supplying, your right to a refund will generally depend on the terms of your agreement.

faq.q: Does Australian Consumer Law protect us with a venue overseas?
faq.a: Do not assume it does. The ACCC guidance describes Australian law, and a venue abroad may contract under local law. Treat the written contract as your protection: deposit, balance dates, currency, postponement and what happens if the venue cannot host.
